solutions.check: 30 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Some baby's malodorous crap

indicators.note: only some of the letters of the following words are taken

parts.note: the letters run on from the end of the first word into the start of the second

explanation.surface: A parent faces a truly foul nappy.
explanation.walkthrough: The nappy picture hides that 'crap' is an adjective here, meaning very poor, and the answer runs straight across 'baby's malodorous'.
explanation.definitionFit: Crap is British slang for dreadfully bad, a plain synonym in informal register.

clue.text: The woman would — for Slough!

parts.note: she = the woman
the contraction of would after a pronoun, as in I'd or you'd

explanation.surface: A woman is willing to do something for Slough, the Berkshire town.
explanation.walkthrough: Slough looks like the Berkshire commuter town, but it is the verb, what a snake does to its old skin; the two pieces read together as she'd.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a snake sloughs its skin in the same sense.

clue.text: One politician finished his shift bankrupt?

definitions.note: used as a verb, to bankrupt someone

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one is I
MP stands for Member of Parliament
over means finished, as in the game is over

indicators.note: to shift is to move about, so these letters change places

explanation.surface: A politician finishes their working day only to find themselves broke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shift' looks like a work shift, but it rearranges HIS into ISH. 'Bankrupt' is the verb here, which the question mark hints at.
explanation.definitionFit: To impoverish is to make someone poor, which is what bankrupting them does.

clue.text: see 18ac.
US writer getting end away? Lecher!

indicators.note: the name gets its end sent away, so its final letter is removed

parts.note: Tom Wolfe was an American novelist and journalist

explanation.surface: A gossip item: an American author caught having it away, branded a lecher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting end away' is British slang for having sex, which suits Private Eye; here it drops the final E of Tom Wolfe's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A wolf is slang for a man who aggressively pursues women, a womaniser or lecher.

clue.text: Hunt no longer takes opportunity to stagger back

definitions.note: Jeremy Hunt held this post until 2024 and no longer does

parts.note: a chance is an opportunity

indicators.note: back means the letters run in reverse order

parts.note: to roll is to sway or stagger, as a sailor does

explanation.surface: A politician named Hunt, out of office, seizes a chance to lurch back into power.
explanation.walkthrough: Jeremy Hunt was the UK's Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) until the 2024 election, so the definition is a former post, not a hunt.
explanation.definitionFit: Jeremy Hunt was Chancellor of the Exchequer until 2024, so he is a chancellor no longer.

clue.text: It's not tender, filthy lucre today, on vacation

indicators.note: filthy suggests the letters are dirtied and jumbled up
a word on vacation is emptied of its middle, leaving only its outer letters

parts.note: the word whose first and last letters are kept

explanation.surface: A grumble that money today has no softness to it, like a cash-hungry holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Filthy lucre' is a stock phrase for money, which hides that 'filthy' is the instruction; 'tender' is the adjective, not legal tender.
explanation.definitionFit: Cruelty is the opposite of tenderness, so it is the quality that is not tender.

clue.text: Arty, virile male, welcomes one after personal problem

indicators.note: the outer word takes the letter in

parts.note: BO = body odour, the classic personal problem

indicators.note: that part comes after the first

parts.note: a he-man is a virile male
I = one, taken inside HE-MAN after the M

explanation.surface: A macho arty type puts up with someone who has a hygiene issue.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads right to left: 'after' means the body-odour piece, though named last, comes first in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an unconventional, artistic way of living.

clue.text: Throttle head off Theresa?

definitions.note: Mother Teresa was the famous nun, so Theresa is a woman known by this title

indicators.note: the head is taken off, so the first letter goes

parts.note: to smother is to choke or throttle

explanation.surface: A satirical urge to throttle Theresa May and take her head off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'head off' drops the S of SMOTHER. The surface points at Theresa May; the question mark flags Mother Teresa, a definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Mother Teresa, the Calcutta nun, carried the title as part of her name.

clue.text: Habit of House leader to leave one on Jack's butt

indicators.note: in a down clue, the first pieces sit on top of the last

parts.note: MANOR = a house, with its first letter removed
a = one
the butt, or tail end, of JACK

explanation.surface: The Leader of the House of Commons has a habit of walking out and leaving someone in the lurch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'House leader' looks parliamentary, but House is a manor and its leader is its first letter. 'Habit' is the clothing sense, as in a nun's habit.
explanation.definitionFit: A habit is a garment, and this hooded weatherproof jacket is one, a definition by example.

clue.text: Blue party — pathetic sort

parts.note: blue = sad
a do = a party

explanation.surface: A Conservative party full of losers.
explanation.walkthrough: Blue is the colour of the Conservative party, so 'Blue party' looks political; it splits into two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for a pathetic, socially inadequate person, a regional informal use.

clue.text: Call on criminal to guarantee funds won't be misused

indicators.note: the first piece is followed by the second

parts.note: to ring = to call on the phone
a fence is a criminal who handles stolen goods

explanation.surface: Someone phones a crook to make sure the money stays clean.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface puts a crook next to money, but 'criminal' is the dealer in stolen goods, and the definition is a finance term, not a crime.
explanation.definitionFit: A budgeting idiom: money protected by an enclosure so it can only be spent on its intended purpose.

clue.text: Offensive type, Roger sags balls

indicators.note: to balls something up is to make a mess of it

parts.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

explanation.surface: A rude joke about an ageing man called Roger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Balls' looks like the body part, fitting the smut, but it is the British 'balls up', to botch or jumble. 'Offensive' means attacking, not rude.
explanation.definitionFit: Offensive in its military sense, attacking: the type who strikes first.

clue.text: Grisly old farmhand — the death of you?

parts.note: grim = grisly
a reaper cut corn by hand in the old days

explanation.surface: A gruesome old farm worker who might finish you off.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that 'the death of you' is the figure of Death himself, the scythe-carrying harvester of souls.
explanation.definitionFit: Death personified comes for everyone, so the idiom 'the death of you' is read literally.

clue.text: Happening straight before Truss's debut

indicators.note: the first piece comes before the second

parts.note: even = straight, level

indicators.note: a debut is a first appearance, so the first letter

parts.note: first letter of TRUSS

explanation.surface: Something happened just before Liz Truss first became Prime Minister.
explanation.walkthrough: Truss is Liz Truss, the briefest-serving UK Prime Minister; her 'debut' is only her first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an occurrence.

clue.text: Minister 'B' caught in mid-denial perhaps

indicators.note: the B goes inside the other letters
the letters are one possible arrangement of the answer

parts.note: anagram fodder with B inside, 10 letters; the hyphen is ignored
the letter itself

explanation.surface: A minister, known only as B, is stuck halfway through denying something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' looks like a hedge but is the anagram indicator; the answer is the former Labour leader who returned to government in 2024.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: he became energy secretary in the 2024 Labour government.

clue.text: Slim sort needs to accept sex is restrictive

indicators.note: the rearranged letters take in the sex word, holding it inside
to sort is to rearrange, so these letters are put in a new order

parts.note: it is a coy word for sex, as in 'doing it'

explanation.surface: A thin person needs to accept that sex has its restrictions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slim sort' reads as a thin type of person, but 'sort' is the instruction acting on 'Slim'; 'it' as sex is a coy euphemism.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that limits sets boundaries on what can happen, i.e. it is restrictive.

clue.text: Big spender wouldn't text part absent member

definitions.note: the definition is a description, 'what a big spender wouldn't do', standing for the verb

parts.note: SCRIPT (a text) without PT, the abbreviation for part
MP = Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A free-spending MP would never skip his lines or his seat.
explanation.walkthrough: PT is the standard abbreviation for part. 'Member' is not a limb but an MP.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by contrast: to economise meanly is the one thing a lavish spender won't do.

clue.text: (& 4dn.) Deputy leader of Alaska turned on crooked air marshal

indicators.note: turned means reversed, so the abbreviation reads backwards

parts.note: AK is the US postal abbreviation for Alaska

indicators.note: crooked means bent out of shape, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A vice-chief from Alaska takes on a corrupt air force officer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned' makes AK into KA, and 'crooked' rearranges AIRMARSHAL into the rest. Kamala Harris was US Vice-President under Joe Biden.
explanation.definitionFit: Kamala Harris served as Vice-President of the United States, a deputy to President Biden.

clue.text: Delay getting Bet screwed in bed

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go inside the bed word

parts.note: the sack is slang for bed, as in hit the sack

indicators.note: screwed means twisted out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A bawdy tale of being held up while Bet was bedded.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface's 'screwed' and 'in bed' are innuendo; 'the sack' is everyday slang for bed.
explanation.definitionFit: A setback is a reversal that holds progress up, a kind of delay.

clue.text: Primary fiasco — Democrat replaces Republican with massive erection

indicators.note: a fiasco is a shambles, so the letters end up in disorder
the Democrat takes the place of the Republican, pushing it out

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for Republican in US politics
D is the abbreviation for Democrat in US politics

explanation.surface: A US primary goes wrong when a Democrat ousts a Republican, with a smutty aside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'replaces' turns one R of PRIMARY into D, giving PDIMARY, and 'fiasco' rearranges those letters. 'Erection' means a building, not the bawdy sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A pyramid is a huge ancient structure, so a massive erection in the sense of something built.

clue.text: Sod the world!

definitions.meaning: sod = turf, a clump of soil with grass

explanation.surface: An exasperated cry of 'to hell with everything!'
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sod' reads as the British curse ('sod it'), but it is a clump of turf.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: soil or turf, and the name of the planet we live on.

clue.text: Soldier wants shag with one knocked out on a routine basis

parts.note: a regular is a professional soldier
LAY = shag; one (A) removed

explanation.surface: A soldier wants sex that leaves somebody flattened.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shag' is British slang for sex; 'one knocked out' reads as a boxing knockout, but it drops the letter A.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: at fixed, habitual intervals.

clue.text: City needs data on eastern state

parts.note: gen = information, data (British slang)
E = eastern
VA = Virginia, a US state

explanation.surface: A city administration asks for figures about an eastern country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State' suggests a nation to match 'eastern', but it is a US state by its postal code; gen is British slang for information.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a Swiss city on the lake of the same name.

clue.text: "Bastard party needs right bloke!"– right-wing Tory

parts.note: b, the polite printed abbreviation of bastard
a rave is a party
R = right, then bloke = man

explanation.surface: An angry cry that the rotten party needs a proper right-winger.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'right' is wordplay; the second belongs to the definition. The answer is the hard-right former Home Secretary, Suella.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a Conservative MP from the party's hard right.

clue.text: Speech on housing that sounds familiar

indicators.note: the words house the answer inside them

parts.note: the letters straddle the two words, dropping the first two and the last

explanation.surface: A speech about the housing crisis sounds like one heard before.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Housing' looks like the policy topic, but it holds the answer inside 'speech on'.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: a sound heard again is, by definition, one you've heard before.

clue.text: Flipping one-time great gets award

indicators.note: the letters are flipped round

parts.note: a = one
T = time
fab = great

explanation.surface: A washed-up star gets a lifetime award, to someone's irritation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' reads as a mild British curse; it reverses the whole string. 'One-time' is split in two.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the British Academy's film and television prize.

clue.text: Panic causes fellow to cover genital area

indicators.note: in a down clue the first piece sits over the second

parts.note: F = fellow
the lap, the area over one's genitals when seated

explanation.surface: A man suddenly panics and covers his crotch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To cover' reads as modesty, but in a down clue it just places the F above the second piece.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal British sense: being 'in a flap' is being flustered.

clue.text: Mediocre cheap housing place providing child care

indicators.note: the words house the answer inside them

parts.note: the last three letters of the first word plus the first three of the second

explanation.surface: Substandard budget housing includes a nursery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Housing' again looks like homes, but it holds the answer inside 'mediocre cheap'.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain descriptive definition of a day nursery, the word borrowed from French.

clue.text: Sun leaving out evil controller

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for Sun, as in Sunday

indicators.note: out means wrong or disordered, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: The sun departs, and a villain is ousted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaving out' reads like 'omitting', but 'leaving' is the fodder and 'out' rearranges it.
explanation.definitionFit: Svengali, the hypnotist in du Maurier's Trilby, gives his name to a sinister manipulator of others.
